In the mathematics of [[permutation]]s, a '''layered permutation''' is a permutation that reverses contiguous blocks of elements. Equivalently, it is the [[Skew and direct sums of permutations|direct sum]] of decreasing permutations.{{r|aepv}}

One of the earlier works establishing the significance of layered permutations was {{harvtxt|Bóna|1999}}, which established the [[Stanley–Wilf conjecture]] for classes of permutations forbidding a layered permutation, before the conjecture was proven more generally.{{r|bona}}

==Example==
For instance, the layered permutations of length four, with the reversed blocks separated by spaces, are the eight permutations
:1 2 3 4
:1 2 43
:1 32 4
:1 432
:21 3 4
:21 43
:321 4
:4321

==Characterization by forbidden patterns==
The layered permutations can also be equivalently described as the permutations that do not contain the [[permutation pattern]]s 231 or 312. That is, no three elements in the permutation (regardless of whether they are consecutive) have the same ordering as either of these forbidden triples.

==Enumeration==
A layered permutation on the numbers from <math>1</math> to <math>n</math> can be uniquely described by the subset of the numbers from <math>1</math> to <math>n-1</math> that are the first element in a reversed block. (The number <math>n</math> is always the first element in its reversed block, so it is redundant for this description.) Because there are <math>2^{n-1}</math> subsets of the numbers from <math>1</math> to <math>n-1</math>, there are also <math>2^{n-1}</math> layered permutation of length <math>n</math>.

The layered permutations are [[Wilf equivalence|Wilf equivalent]] to other permutation classes, meaning that the numbers of permutations of each length are the same. For instance, the [[Gilbreath permutation]]s are counted by the same function <math>2^{n-1}</math>.{{r|rob}}

==Superpatterns==
The shortest [[superpattern]] of the layered permutations of length <math>n</math> is itself a layered permutation. Its length is a [[sorting number]], the number of comparisons needed for [[Insertion sort|binary insertion sort]] to sort <math>n+1</math> elements.{{r|aepv|gray}} For <math>n=1,2,3,\dots</math> these numbers are
:1, 3, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 21, 25, 29, 33, 37, ... {{OEIS|A001855}}
and in general they are given by the formula
:<math>(n+1)\bigl\lceil\log_2 (n+1)\bigr\rceil - 2^{\left\lceil\log_2 (n+1)\right\rceil} + 1.</math>{{r|aepv}}

==Related permutation classes==
Every layered permutation is an [[Involution (mathematics)|involution]]. They are exactly the 231-avoiding involutions, and they are also exactly the 312-avoiding involutions.{{r|em}}

The layered permutations are a subset of the [[stack-sortable permutation]]s, which forbid the pattern 231 but not the pattern 312.
Like the stack-sortable permutations, they are also a subset of the [[separable permutation]]s, the permutations formed by recursive combinations of direct and skew sums.
